power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<0.05", Text = "Descriptive analyses and parametric statistical tests (ANOVA and Tukey, p<0.05) were applied."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

text.text: Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) represents a global public health threat, with a rising prevalence, particularly among vulnerable populations.

This cross-sectional study analyzed MDR-TB notifications in Brazil from 2001 to 2021, using data from DATASUS, and stratified by periods and risk groups (HIV-positive individuals, smokers, drug users, healthcare workers, incarcerated individuals, and people experiencing homelessness).
Descriptive analyses and parametric statistical tests (ANOVA and Tukey, p<0.05) were applied.
text.formatted: Descriptive analyses and parametric statistical tests (ANOVA and Tukey, p<0.05) were applied.

text.text: A significant increase in cases was observed across all groups, especially between 2017 and 2021, with growth ranging from 294% to 574% depending on the population.
Factors such as treatment abandonment, coinfection, social vulnerability, and occupational exposure were key determinants for MDR-TB dissemination.

The findings indicate that current public health policies are insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for targeted prevention strategies, therapeutic follow-up, and control measures for high-risk populations.
Tuberculosis (TB) is a notifiable infectious disease worldwide caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis¹.
It is a life-threatening condition that has afflicted humanity since ancient times, contributing substantially to morbidity and mortality².
Currently, the World Health Organization (WHO) classifies TB as a high-risk disease for humanity and considers it one of the leading threats to global public health.

The WHO estimates that approximately 10 million people become infected with the disease, with about 6.4 million individuals diagnosed with TB, and that it causes approximately 1.6 million deaths worldwide³.
According to the United Nations (UN), 95% of cases occur in underdeveloped countries⁴.

Brazil has faced persistent challenges related to TB for and vulnerable groups, including people experiencing homelessness, individuals with substance use disorders, persons deprived of liberty, individuals living with HIV or those who are immunocompromised, and healthcare workers.

Thus, the study was designed as a population-based investigation using descriptive statistical analysis to characterize demographic and treatment-related variables, including tuberculosis-related complications in Brazil.
Temporal analyses were performed over the period from 2001 to 2021, with data analyzed in their entirety.

Additionally, the study period was subdivided into four intervals-first period (2001-2006), second period (2007-2011), third period (2012-2016), and fourth period (2017-2021)-to assess changes in the epidemiological profile of the disease over time.
All analyzed data were presented as means and standard deviations, adopting a significance threshold of p< 0.05.
text.formatted: All analyzed data were presented as means and standard deviations, adopting a significance threshold of p< 0.05.

text.text: Data were tabulated using Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Office Professional Plus, 2016; Microsoft).
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 6.0.
Graphical data presentation was generated using GraphPad Prism 6.0 and the Departamento de Informática do Sistema Único de Saúde (DATASUS) platform (2023).
Normality was assessed for all variables using the D'Agostino-Pearson test or the Shapiro-Wilk test.
Parametric tests were applied for group comparisons (one-way ANOVA), with confirmation by Tukey's post hoc test.
A significance level of p < 0.05 was adopted.
text.formatted: A significance level of p < 0.05 was adopted.

text.text: All data and graphical outputs were analyzed and presented as means and standard deviations.
Source: Authors' own elaboration Between 2001 and 2021, a total of 1,620 cases of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis were reported among patients living with HIV in Brazil.
The lowest mean number of cases was observed during the period from 2001 to 2006, whereas the highest mean was reported between 2017 and 2021 (1008.00 ± 97.09 cases).
Notably, the last evaluated period showed a 574% increase compared with the beginning of the time series.
The periods from 2012 to 2016 and from 2017 to 2021 demonstrated a statistically significant difference (p < 0.0001) compared with the other periods.
text.formatted: The periods from 2012 to 2016 and from 2017 to 2021 demonstrated a statistically significant difference (p < 0.0001) compared with the other periods.

text.text: Source: Authors' own elaboration Between 2001 and 2021, a total of 1,620 cases of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis were reported in Brazil.
The lowest mean number of cases was observed during the period from 2001 to 2006 (3.2 ± 5.60 cases), whereas the highest mean was reported between 2017 and 2021 (150.4 ± 19.76 cases).
During the period from 2007 to 2011, a mean of 27.4 ± 16.65 cases was observed, and between 2016 and 2021, a mean of 144.00 ± 39.73 cases was recorded.
The periods from 2012 to 2016 and from 2017 to 2021 showed a statistically significant difference (p < 0.0001) compared with the other periods.

text.text: Source: Authors' own elaboration Between 2001 and 2021, a total of 7,554 cases of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis were reported in Brazil.
The lowest mean number of cases was observed during the period from 2001 to 2006 (2.00 ± 1.86 cases), whereas the highest mean was reported between 2017 and 2021 (1048.20 ± 146.73 cases).

Notably, the last evaluated period showed a 326% increase compared with the period from 2012 to 2016.
The period from 2017 to 2021 demonstrated a statistically significant difference (p < 0.0001) compared with the other periods.

text.text: Furthermore, cases reported during the period from 2017 to 2021 accounted for 71.04% of the total.
Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is considered a global health problem, with a prevalence of 11.6%¹⁶.
Over the past two decades, Brazil has experienced a significant increase in the number of cases, as shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Over the past two decades, Brazil has experienced a significant increase in the number of cases, as shown in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: The rate of resistance to at least one drug between 2003 and 2006 was 12.4%².
This increase is strongly associated with multiple risk factors and the country's socioeconomic conditions⁷.
Individuals who live or work in environments with a high bacillary load, poor ventilation, and overcrowding are more susceptible to acquiring the disease¹⁷.

An important property of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB), compared with drug-susceptible TB, is its greater transmissibility, which represents an increased risk of dissemination and a major concern for public health authorities¹⁸.

Drug-resistant TB may develop as a result of deficiencies in treatment adherence, including poor compliance, treatment abandonment, inappropriate treatment regimen selection, or inadequate drug supply.

The management of MDR-TB cases is challenging, particularly in the presence of cavitary lesions and caseous granulomas that harbor subpopulations of bacilli, some exhibiting phenotypic resistance despite genetic susceptibility (non-heritable resistance that regresses after antibiotic withdrawal), while others present genetic mutations associated with both phenotypic and heritable resistance⁴³.
A general analysis of the present study's findings indicates a persistent increase in the incidence and prevalence of MDR-TB cases over time, as illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: A general analysis of the present study's findings indicates a persistent increase in the incidence and prevalence of MDR-TB cases over time, as illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: This increase occurs particularly among populations considered vulnerable, including persons deprived of liberty, people experiencing homelessness, individuals with substance use disorders, smokers, and people living with HIV/AIDS.
A study conducted by Ridolfi and colleagues analyzed the biological and behavioral factors associated with each component of unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes.
Among the total number of participants, 13% did not achieve successful treatment outcomes.
Among these individuals, a common and prominent characteristic was being people living with HIV.

Furthermore, the study identified that behavioral factors, such as current drug use and tobacco consumption, were more strongly associated with loss to follow-up, whereas clinical comorbidities, such as HIV and diabetes, were more closely associated with treatment failure and death.

Therefore, intervention strategies focused on health education, support for substance use treatment, and management of comorbidities may be particularly effective in reducing these unfavorable outcomes²⁰.

A study by Coelho and colleagues confirmed this hypothesis, demonstrating a significant increase in MDR-TB cases among patients living with HIV, with approximately 50% of patients diagnosed with drug-resistant TB being HIV-positive.
These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure 2, which showed a significant increase in the number of cases²¹.
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>, which showed a significant increase in the number of cases²¹.

text.text: Additionally, these patients presented with a higher frequency of cavitary pulmonary lesions and more frequent changes in treatment regimens.

The increase in MDR-TB among patients living with HIV or AIDS is not solely related to immune system impairment, but also to the fact that these individuals are often already receiving multiple long-term medications with substantial adverse effects.
This circumstance may hinder adherence to additional daily medications that must be incorporated into their routine for prolonged periods during tuberculosis treatment²².
Since 1918, smoking has been identified as a risk factor for tuberculosis, with exposure to smoke being substantially associated with TB recurrence and increased mortality.
Studies indicate that more than 1.3 billion smokers live in underdeveloped or developing countries, where tuberculosis rates are also higher²³.
These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure 3, which demonstrates an increase in the number of cases over time.
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>, which demonstrates an increase in the number of cases over time.

text.text: This association may be explained by the fact that smoking alters the defense mechanisms of the bronchial tree and reduces blood oxygen concentration, contributing to the severity of necrotizing lesions and delaying tissue repair, factors that may lead to the development of more severe disease manifestations.

Cigarette smoke plays a role in disease pathogenesis by promoting ciliary dysfunction and reducing immune responses through impaired macrophage activity, thereby increasing susceptibility to mycobacterial infection²⁴.

Smoking increases the risk of latent and active TB, false-negative results and delays in sputum testing, reduces treatment adherence, and increases recurrence rates; collectively, these factors contribute to the development of multidrug-resistant disease²⁵.

Although healthcare workers are not considered a neglected population, they remain a high-risk group for MDR-TB, as their occupational environment involves frequent contact with bacilliferous patients, including those who do not adhere adequately to treatment.
This risk is reflected in the annual tuberculin skin test conversion rate, which ranges from 2.2% to 5.6%²⁶.

Such tuberculin conversion is primarily attributed to nosocomial exposure to patients with pulmonary TB, the absence or inadequacy of individual or collective biosafety measures, and is particularly notable among nursing professionals²⁷.
In this context, tuberculosis is classified as a notifiable occupational disease.
An aggravating factor is that these workers, in addition to exposure to bacilliferous patients, are also exposed to other infectious conditions affecting patients.

According to the manual of recommendations for tuberculosis control, nursing professionals present the highest risk among healthcare workers, with rates 3 to 20 times higher than those of the general population, followed by clinical pathologists (6-11 times), laboratory technicians (2-9 times), and pulmonologists (6 times)²⁸.
The data presented in this study demonstrate a significant increase in MDR-TB notifications among healthcare workers during the period from 2017 to 2021.
This finding may be explained by underreporting in previous years, as well as by the lack of effective interconnection between health information systems²⁰.

The prison population is of particular concern to public health authorities, as it represents a group characterized by multiple vulnerabilities, including HIV infection, alcohol consumption, and the use of illicit drugs and tobacco, with a growing trend in substance use²⁹.

Furthermore, poor living conditions in correctional facilities, such as overcrowded shared cells, inadequate ventilation, limited exposure to sunlight, and insufficient healthcare services, predispose individuals to the transmission of TB and its drug-resistant forms⁵⁰.
These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure 5, which demonstrates an increase in MDR-TB rates within this population.
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>, which demonstrates an increase in MDR-TB rates within this population.

text.text: Additionally, alcoholism and AIDS have also been identified as important risk factors, as they may weaken the immune system and hinder adherence to TB treatment³¹.
Another critical factor identified was a history of previous TB treatment among persons deprived of liberty.

Individuals who have undergone prior treatment have an increased risk of developing drug-resistant TB, particularly when previous treatment was not completed adequately or when interruptions occurred in the therapeutic regimen³².
Individuals experiencing homelessness are 56 times more likely to be affected by tuberculosis, as they are exposed to multiple vulnerabilities³³.
This finding is consistent with the data presented in Figure 6, which demonstrates an increase in MDR-TB rates within this population.
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with the data presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">6</ref>, which demonstrates an increase in MDR-TB rates within this population.

text.text: Due to limited financial resources, this group makes less frequent use of healthcare services, resulting in delayed diagnosis, which may lead to poor treatment adherence and unfavorable outcomes³⁴.
In this context, progression to drugresistant forms of the disease becomes more likely.
Individuals affected by TB tend to experience unsuccessful treatment outcomes due to factors such as intravenous drug use, alcohol consumption, malnutrition, and HIV coinfection.
This association is supported by the findings of the present study, which identified a positive intrinsic relationship between high-risk populations and MDR-TB³⁵.
Furthermore, for people experiencing homelessness, concerns such as safety, access to food, and the need for rest often compete with attention to healthcare needs³⁶.

Individuals with substance use disorders constitute one of the socially marginalized groups requiring special attention in healthcare, as they accumulate multiple risk factors beyond illicit drug use, including a higher likelihood of experiencing homelessness, acquiring infectious diseases through needle sharing, and concurrent dependence on licit substances such as tobacco and alcohol³⁷.
These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure 7, which illustrates an increase in MDR-TB rates within this population.
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with the data presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">7</ref>, which illustrates an increase in MDR-TB rates within this population.

text.text: A study conducted by Kazempour and colleagues demonstrated that 65.7% of patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis who died were male and smokers, and 50% were drug users³⁷.
It is noteworthy that estimates indicate that more than 15% of deaths associated with tuberculosis could be prevented if patients did not engage in heavy alcohol consumption³⁸.

Data from another study suggest that individuals with alcohol use disorder are nearly four times more likely to discontinue tuberculosis treatment, with the main reasons for treatment abandonment being a perceived sense of well-being and adverse effects resulting from the combined use of medications with alcohol and other drugs³⁹.
Furthermore, even when access to healthcare services is facilitated, adherence to long-term treatment among individuals with substance use disorders remains a significant challenge³ 8.
text.formatted: Furthermore, even when access to healthcare services is facilitated, adherence to long-term treatment among individuals with substance use disorders remains a significant challenge³ <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref>.

text.text: An analysis of all the figures in the present study indicates that the period from 2001 to 2011 showed the lowest MDR-TB rates, which may be explained by the existence of multiple health information systems that were not integrated at the time.

This scenario changed in 2013 with the establishment of the Departamento de Informática do Sistema Único de Saúde (DATASUS), which unified the country's compulsory disease notification information system 39.
text.formatted: This scenario changed in 2013 with the establishment of the Departamento de Informática do Sistema Único de Saúde (DATASUS), which unified the country's compulsory disease notification information system <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref>.

text.text: Based on the data analysis, it can be concluded that in recent years there has been an overall increase in the number of MDR-TB cases across all high-risk populations studied in Brazil.
This increase highlights the limitations of current public health policies aimed at controlling this disease.
The higher prevalence of MDR-TB may be attributed to treatment abandonment, poor socioeconomic conditions, and inadequate patient follow-up within the healthcare system.
In this context, the findings underscore the urgent need to strengthen public health policies directed at combating this condition.

The main limitations identified in conducting this study included the initial absence of a centralized database compiling all notifications and, even after the establishment of the Departamento de Informática do Sistema Único de Saúde (DATASUS), the incomplete migration of these data to the new platform.
Additional limitations included underreporting of cases among healthcare workers prior to 2017 and the inability to perform internal data linkage within the system.
